articles.headline: Nominating Convention.
articles.text:
Nominating Convention.

A convention of the citizens and qualified voters of Billings county, will be held Monday evening, March 1, 1886, to place in nomination a list of county officers to be voted for on the second Monday in April, 1886 and to hold office until the next regular fall election. A full attendance is requested.
articles.summary: Call for a Billings County nominating convention on March 1, 1886, to nominate county officers for the April election.

articles.headline: Mandan Water Works.
articles.text:
Mandan Water Works.

The Mandan Pioneer makes a characteristic answer to the charge made in our last issue against the Mandan water works system. The article occupies a column in the Pioneer; most completely begs the question and while showing to every one that our position, as published in the Bismarck Tribune was right, as clearly shows that the Pioneer lacks the backbone to come out boldly and acknowledge it.

The controversy, if carried on according to the plan of the Pioneer, would be as endless as it would be uninteresting to our readers. We merely ask the Pioneer to deny the following statements and that the history of the Mandan water works shows great negligence, if not actual fraud, for the following reasons:

1. There never was a contract let, nor did the council vote on the question. The proposal of a former partner was accepted by the Mayor.

2. Other proposals were not considered. Notably the one of a perfectly responsible company who offered to erect necessary buildings and constantly supply Mandan with water for domestic and fire purposes. Their bid was only a few thousand, two or three, we think more than the accepted proposal, which only offered water for fire purposes.

3. Full price was paid the contractor, although he put in cheaper and inferior water pipes to those mentioned in his proposal.

4. The supply of water came only from the Northern Pacific tanks and only a verbal agreement was had with an officer of the company that they would furnish the town with water in case of fire.

5. There has been at no time a guarantee of sufficient water even for fire purposes.

The above and twenty other minor charges were the points we urged two years ago against the Mandan water works. There is no use asking the Pioneer to deny them for they are absolute facts, known to all. That the Pioneer begs the question in its answer to our article is shown by the fact that its strongest point is made on the supposition that the present water works in Mandan are thought to have kept the fire from spreading and thus saved a loss of $60,000 or more. We are almost ashamed to answer such a statement, which we will do, however, by a question: "Would not the better system we have advocated saved as much as this poorer system."

In conclusion we will add that a system of water works which would have furnished water in abundance for domestic and fire purposes, would have paid for itself already in actual cash in a reduction of insurance rates and by the collections for water privileges.

We beg pardon of our readers for having taken up space for the discussion of a question that in no wise interests them or us and as we know the Pioneer cannot answer our statements, leave the matter for the Mandanites to fight out among themselves.
articles.summary: Packard answers the Mandan Pioneer over the Mandan water works, listing charges of negligence or fraud, then drops the matter.

articles.text: The anti-Chinese agitation at Seattle has reached the culminating point. Sunday morning a large body of men raided the Chinese quarter and compelled them to go bag and baggage on board a steamer bound for San Francisco. The city officers attempted to stop the eviction but were powerless.
articles.summary: Brief national item on the expulsion of Chinese residents from Seattle.

articles.text: Edward Payson Weston on last Saturday night, finished his long tramp of 2,500 miles in fifty-four days. It was a test case wherein Weston represented total abstinence and Dan O'Leary the whiskey men. Temperance won and Weston is to receive a purse of $2,000 from his prohibition friends in New York.
articles.summary: Brief national item: pedestrian Edward Payson Weston finished a 2,500-mile walk, beating Dan O'Leary.

articles.text: Mr. S. Pelton of Dickinson, recently gave a correspondent of the Mandan Pioneer some useful information relative to the thermometer and the correspondent waxed wroth thereat. We don't like to mix in such family jars, but we suggest as a good subject for the correspondent's next effort the following words which recently appeared in one of Mr. Pelton's letters; "My thermometer is placed where it is sheltered from the wind." This is the first intimation we have had that wind effects a thermometer.
articles.summary: Packard pokes fun at a thermometer quarrel between S. Pelton of Dickinson and a Mandan Pioneer correspondent.

articles.text: As mentioned in our last issue, we to-day issue the call for a nominating convention. We have spoken to a number of citizens and all agreed that March 1 would be the best time to hold the convention as sufficient notice can be given to all and it leaves nearly five weeks between the nominating convention and April 5, the day of election. Although every one spoken to, agreed that March 1, was the best date to hold the nominating convention, it was thought unnecessary to obtain signatures to a call, for the reason that no man or body of men had authority in the matter and the list must of necessity be incomplete unless it contained the name of every voter in the county.
articles.summary: Packard explains why March 1 was chosen for the nominating convention and why the call carries no signatures.

articles.text: There seems to be perfect unanimity of feeling in regard to the stockmen nominating two of the commissioners. We suggest that it would be a good plan for the cattlemen to hold a caucus before the nominating convention on March 1 and then present the names of their nominees to the convention for confirmation. It could be easily arranged in the afternoon of March 1, or in the evening before the convention.
articles.summary: Packard suggests the stockmen caucus before the March 1 convention to name two county commissioners.

articles.text: General Hancock died Tuesday afternoon on Governor's Island. His death was a great shock and surprise to his family and friends, being [entirely?] unexpected. He died of kidney disease. Gen. Hancock was one of the most gallant soldiers of the rebellion and an unsuccessful candidate for the Presidency in 1880. His successor as Major General will be one of Generals Schofield, Terry or Howard.
articles.summary: National item reporting the death of Gen. Winfield S. Hancock on Governor's Island.

articles.text: The true reason why President Cleveland refuses to give reasons for removals from office, appears to be that he is protecting politicians who in many instances have trumped up false charges against perfectly honest and competent officials. To be true to his civil service principles, he must give reasons, and good ones, for every removal. It looks as though any reason had been accepted whenever a ward striker wanted a position and that the President has placed himself in a bad situation. Either he must give up all pretension of civil service reform or expose the lies of his political friends.
articles.summary: Editorial criticizing President Cleveland's refusal to give reasons for removals from office.

articles.text: It seems scarcely necessary to remind every one of the duty they owe themselves and the county to attend the nominating convention to be held here March 1. In spite of all that can be said or done there will be those who will stay away from the convention and then kick against the ticket or a portion of it. It is every voter's duty to attend both the convention and the election and he fails just that much in performing his duty if he stay away from either. No perfectly representative ticket can be nominated without the attendance of all or nearly all of Billings' voters.
articles.summary: Packard urges every Billings County voter to attend the March 1 convention and the election.

articles.text: The day of good prices for thin or half-ripe cattle is over. At least the Chicago market points to such a conclusion. Cattle in good condition and weighing over 1,200 pounds hold their price well, but prices on poor animals are totally demoralized. According to the Inter Ocean, there have been 5,000 steers sold at $4 and below, to every one sold over $5.50.
articles.summary: Chicago market shows thin cattle prices demoralized while heavy cattle hold their price.

articles.text:
In a note to the editor, Mr. Stafford, our representative at the Denver convention, writes of the subject of branding cattle:

"Mr. Light's paper on branding cattle was very good, but in talking with the cattlemen I learn their position is that they do not feel it incumbent upon them to tear their tunics over a change in the present system of branding till there is more difference in the price paid for hides with brands and hides without brands, and that whenever the distinction is made in price that Mr. Light claims exists in value of the hides, they are ready to pay some attention to proposed changes in branding. A prominent Southwest Texas cattle owner told me that he shipped a large lot of hides from the Indian Territory, some with very light brands, and others burned all over and that there was no distinction."—[Texas Stockman.
articles.summary: Reprint from the Texas Stockman: cattlemen at the Denver convention see no reason to change branding until branded hides fetch less.

articles.text: There is a style of cow boy very rare, let it be said to the credit of the guild, who think it smart to "shoot up" a town, though of late several of these smart Alecs have had their cowardly carcasses punctured with cold lead, and this amusement is not so popular with them as of yore. Of late, terrorizing passenger trains is a favorite pastime with them, and there it is, among women, children and unarmed men, that their peculiar style of bravery (?) finds full scope. There they can insult ladies, frighten children, terrorize train men to their heart's content, and who is there to make them afraid. Some time they will make one of these plays in the presence of a sure enough cowboy, one of the sort that attends to his own business, takes off his hat to ladies even in a smoking car, and if he wants a row, hunts up some one in the same humor, and then these bad men from away high up on Bitter Creek will receive a deposit of more cold lead where it will do the most good, and a jury of decent citizens will say amen.—[Texas Stockman.
articles.summary: Reprint from the Texas Stockman condemning the rare cowboy who "shoots up" towns and terrorizes passenger trains.

articles.headline: How to Break a Broncho.
articles.text:
How to Break a Broncho.

"How do you break bronchos?" asked a reporter of a well-known horseman.

"Why, sometimes we use an axe and sometimes a stone-crusher," replied the horseman, who was real funny when he felt good natured.

"No, but seriously, how is the work of getting a broncho into the state of being, whereby he becomes like an every-day gentle horse accomplished?" asked the reporter, who was searching for information on an important subject, rather than for gems of American humor.

"Well, sir," said the [horseman as he?] closed one eye and looked critically at a thoroughbred bull pup, "when you come to that, a broncho never becomes like a well-behaved horse until he is ready to drop into his grave or the hands of the rendering works people.

"When a broncho gets so that he behaves himself decently all the time, if you own him, you had better sell him, for you can bet your life he has his will made and is going to croak soon. A broncho is only a pony, a kind of small horse and so we try to break him in the same way we use in breaking a colt. But the difference between the two animals is that a colt will always be wild and more or less mischievous at first, while a broncho is always vicious and full of deviltry that can never be taken out of him.

"All bronchos," continued the horseman in a meditative tone, as he slowly scratched the bull pup's head with the end of a whip-stock, "stand toward the common horses very much as the Devil does toward mankind.

"You know that all men and women and kids have more or less wickedness in 'em, but Old Nick is just chock full of cussedness. Once in a while Beelzebub may pretend to show a little bit of goodness, but it's just for a blind. He's always got some scheme in it. And that's just the way with the bronchos."

"A mule is an angel of light alongside a broncho, chimed in a hostler, who had been listening to the conversation.

"That's so," agreed the horseman, "I used to own a pair of the handsomest mules that ever set foot in Colorado, and they were pretty well-behaved for mules too. Well, I've known one of those mules, when I was driving 'em double, to kick out and hit a dog in the road twelve feet behind him and never lose step with his mate. Do you want to buy a broncho, Mister?"

The visitor jingled two lonesome nickels in his pocket and modestly replied in the negative.

"Because if you did," the horseman continued, "I've got the only broncho in this stable that ever really was broken and he's a pretty little beast too. But if you only want to know for the curiosity of it, I'll tell you how we break them.

"The first thing is to catch one. You know they run wild like other colts until we get ready to try and use 'em. Unless you use a lariat, you'll find that catching a broncho in the field or even in a corrall, is no spiritualist's picnic. When you've got him you must mount him and that ain't no coming home from the picnic by moonlight, neither.

"He will dance and kick and kick and dance like all posessed. If you are patient he will stop still enough for you to get near enough to get on, after a little while, say about an hour. Of course he's got no idea what you want to do, for nobody ever tried that on him before."

"So as soon as you make a jump he'll jump sideways about eight or ten feet, and if you've got him by a halter or a lariat he'll jerk you about twenty feet unless you let go. If you do let go you'll not catch him again for about a week unless you've been doing all this in a brick building. If its any other kind of a building he'll kick the side of it out and get away."

"Suppose that you get on him finally, you won't need a bridle the first time; just grab him by the hair and lay down. If you can, get your feet locked underneath him at the same time. If you were nailed onto him, he'd get you off in a few minutes anyway, but you have to give him as much of a tussle as you can."

"The first thing he'll do is to run like lightning, and shake himself from side to side. A part of the time he'll run sideways, and a part backwards, and now and then he'll go a little ways straight ahead. If you keep on all this time he'll stop suddenly when he's going full tilt, with all four legs stiff as iron bars. If that dont throw you off his back, it'll jerk your entrails into your mouth. I've seen a man thrown twenty or thirty feet off a broncho's back before now."

"For the first lesson all you can do is to try and keep on him as long and as often as possible. After you've done this several days you can try and get a bridle on him and bits into his mouth. You'll have a circus getting them fixed, and another one when you try a saddle, and a side show attached when you try to hitch him to a wagon, but all you've got to do is to make him know that you intend to be boss, and in time, if you are patient enough, you'll get your broncho as [near?] broken as it's possible to break one of the nasty little cusses."—[Denver Tribune-Republican.
articles.summary: Humorous reprint from the Denver Tribune-Republican in which a horseman explains how bronchos are broken.

articles.summary: Rev. Wm. Cooke of Gladstone will preach at the Medora depot next Sunday afternoon.

articles.summary: Strayed cattle of many Little Missouri brands near Dickinson are being rounded up and returned to the Badlands.

articles.text: Vol. III, No. 1, of the COW BOY, appears this issue. As a three-year-old, we hope to put on more (financial) fat, than has come to our lot in the yearling and two-year-old periods and our readers can be certain that the COW BOY will strive harder than ever to give value received.
articles.summary: Packard marks the start of the Cow Boy's third volume and promises to strive harder to give value.

articles.text: A flood came down the river very unexpectedly yesterday, reaching Medora a little before twelve. To-day it has gone down but little, if any and it is impossible to ford it. Large cakes of bottom ice are seen occasionally and it would not be surprising if the annual break-up should begin any time.
articles.summary: An unexpected flood came down the Little Missouri to Medora; the river cannot be forded and the ice break-up may begin.

articles.text: Saturday and Sunday were two as perfect days as could be imagined. The thermometer ranged about sixty degrees above, and Saturday it reached seventy-five. The warm weather extended far south, as is shown by the immense volume of snow water now pouring down on the ice.
articles.summary: Unusually warm weekend weather, reaching 75 degrees on Saturday, sent snow water down onto the river ice.

articles.text: Lloyd Roberts and Tommy Skinner started for Cave Hills Tuesday night. Lloyd will start east soon to buy cattle on contracts he has already secured and may buy for Aleck Connell, who has bought out Gallup's Cave Hills ranch and will stock it this season. Tommy Skinner will again go to "cow-punching" in Aleck's employ.
articles.summary: Lloyd Roberts and Tommy Skinner left for the Cave Hills; Aleck Connell has bought Gallup's Cave Hills ranch and will stock it.

articles.text: It appears that the Rev. Schaffner was allowed to leave the country, in spite of the fact that he was sentenced to six months in the penitentiary. He was said to have chopped a large amount of wood north of Dickinson for his son to sell this winter and then bade good-bye to the banana belt and returned to his beloved Canada. The ways of justice in Dakota are sometimes very dubious.
articles.summary: Rev. Schaffner, sentenced to six months in the penitentiary, was allowed to leave for Canada.

articles.text: Hitherto there has been but little delay in local subscribers paying up and we hope to have a large number of renewals during the coming week. The subscriptions of all who have taken the COW BOY from the beginning, become delinquent with this issue. Bring in your two dollars for 1886.
articles.summary: Packard asks subscribers to renew for 1886 as original subscriptions expire with this issue.

articles.text:
Stock Inspector Fred Willard, of Medora, D. T., is in the city. He came 1,500 miles for a horse thief whom a local officer assured him by wire that he had here. The local officer had the thief in his eye, but when he undertook to place him in limbo the fellow wouldn't have it and drawing his gun, escaped.

The above article, taken from the Rapid City Republican, is a meagre report of the attempted capture of "Calamity Joe." It seems that the deputy who tried to make the arrest is generally so full of whiskey that he dont know the difference between a pair of handcuffs and a search-warrant and while fumbling in his pockets for the former, "Calamity Joe" drew a revolver and stood the deputy off. When Fred arrived in Rapid, Joe had skipped the country and was nowhere to be found. Fred reached Medora last night and offers a reward of $100. for "Calamity's" arrest or information leading to it.
articles.summary: Stock Inspector Fred Willard went to Rapid City after horse thief "Calamity Joe," who escaped a deputy; Willard returned and offers a $100 reward.

articles.headline: Notice of Election.
articles.text:
Notice of Election.

Notice is hereby given that on the Second (2nd.) Monday in April, 1886, at the following place, viz.: at the town of MEDORA, in the County of Billings, an election will be held for the following officers of said county of Billings, in said Territory of Dakota, in the organization of said county;

Three County Commissioners,
One Register of Deeds,
One County Clerk,
One Sheriff,
One Assessor,
One Judge of Probate,
One County Treasurer,
One County Surveyor,
One Coroner,
One Superintendent of Public Schools,
Four Justices of the Peace,
Four Constables,
and also for the temporary location of the County seat of said county,
which election will be open at the hour of eight o'clock in the morning and will continue open until five o'clock in the afternoon of the same day.

Dated this [20th?] day of January, 1886.

GILBERT A. PIERCE, Governor.
{SEAL.}
M. L. MCCORMACK, Secretary.
articles.summary: Governor Gilbert A. Pierce's proclamation of the election at Medora on the second Monday of April 1886 to organize Billings County and locate its temporary county seat.
